## Overview

-   **Input:** `data/IMvigor210_plain.rds` (TPM and clinical tables;
    this file does not need script 01 to be run first)
-   **Output:** figures in `results/figures/` (`gep_*.png`)
-   **Comparison:** complete response (R, n = 25) vs progressive disease
    (NR, n = 167).

## 0. Setup

```{r}
# Set up working directory

root <- ".."
fig_dir <- file.path(root, "results", "figures")
dir.create(fig_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| warning: false
# Load libraries and data

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

d        <- readRDS(file.path(root, "data", "IMvigor210_plain.rds"))
tpm      <- as.matrix(d$tpm)
counts   <- as.matrix(d$counts)
clinical <- as.data.frame(d$clinical)
```

```{r}
# Basic data processing

clinical$BOR <- factor(clinical$BOR, levels = c("NR", "R"))
clinical$resp <- as.integer(clinical$BOR == "R") # a numeric flag for responders

rownames(clinical) <- clinical$sample_id

logtpm <- log2(tpm + 1)

# Make sure patients are in the same order in the expression matrix and the clinical table
logtpm <- logtpm[, clinical$sample_id]

table(clinical$BOR)
```

## Task 1: Identify the 18 GEP genes and examine their expression in the dataset

In the paper from Ayers et al. the GEP list consists in the following
list:

```{r}
# GEP genes

GEP_genes <- c(
  "CD27", "CD274", "PDCD1", "CD276", "CD8A", "CMKLR1",
  "CXCL9", "CXCR6", "HLA-DQA1", "HLA-DRB1", "HLA-E",
  "IDO1", "LAG3", "NKG7", "PDCD1LG2", "PSMB10", "STAT1", "TIGIT"
)
```

Note: this is the list from Exercise 6. The list published by Ayers et
al. (2017) has CCL5 instead of PDCD1. We keep the course list here

```{r}
# Are genes present?

GEP_genes_present <- GEP_genes[GEP_genes %in% rownames(tpm)]

cat("GEP genes present:", length(GEP_genes_present), "of", length(GEP_genes), "\n")
```

All genes are present in the dataset (hopefully!!). Let's focus on their
expression now

We use log2(TPM + 1) and not raw counts. TPM is corrected for sequencing
depth and gene length, so values can be compared between patients. The
log makes the distribution less skewed.

```{r}
# Extract GEP genes expression in the dataset

X <- logtpm[GEP_genes_present, , drop = FALSE]   # 18 genes x 192 patients

# Median expression of each gene across all patients
sort(round(apply(X, 1, median), 2), decreasing = TRUE)
```

```{r}
# Expression of the 18 GEP genes in responders vs non-responders

R  <- clinical$BOR == "R"
NR <- clinical$BOR == "NR"

gene_tab <- data.frame(
  gene      = rownames(X),
  mean_R    = rowMeans(X[, R]),
  mean_NR   = rowMeans(X[, NR]),
  log2FC    = rowMeans(X[, R]) - rowMeans(X[, NR]),   # difference of log2 values = log2 fold change
  p_value   = apply(X, 1, function(x) wilcox.test(x[R], x[NR])$p.value)
)
gene_tab$FDR <- p.adjust(gene_tab$p_value, method = "BH")   # correct for 18 tests

# Sort the genes by p-value (most different first)
gene_tab <- gene_tab[order(gene_tab$p_value), ]
rownames(gene_tab) <- NULL
knitr::kable(gene_tab, digits = 3)
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
# Boxplots of each gene, R vs NR

long <- data.frame(
  gene = factor(rep(rownames(X), times = ncol(X)), levels = gene_tab$gene),
  expr = as.vector(X),
  BOR  = rep(clinical$BOR, each = nrow(X))
)

p_genes <- ggplot(long, aes(BOR, expr, fill = BOR)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.5, alpha=0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, size = 0.4, alpha = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ gene, scales = "free_y", ncol = 6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(NR = "grey70", R = "#D55E00")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "log2(TPM + 1)") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
p_genes
ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "gep_genes_boxplots.png"), p_genes, width = 10, height = 8, dpi = 300)
```

**Analysis:** Most of the GEP genes are overexpressed in responders:
only CD276 and HLA-DQA1 aren't (log2FC close to 0). They are also the
two bottom ranked genes in the table, which is sorted by p-value. All
genes also have a significant FDR, less than 0.05, except these two
genes and HLA-DRB1, the third from the bottom.

## 2. Calculate a GEP score for each patient

For this task, we use the scoring from the course (also from exercise
6): standardise each gene across patients (z-score), then average the 18
z-scores for each patient. Standardising first gives every gene the same
weight, so highly expressed genes such as HLA-E or STAT1 do not
dominate.

```{r}
# GEP score

Z <- t(scale(t(X)))          # z-score each gene across patients
clinical$GEP <- colMeans(Z)

summary(clinical$GEP)
```

Let's try to reproduce the heatmap from the paper, with the 18 genes
ordered by GEP score

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.5
# Z-scored expression of the 18 GEP genes. Patients are sorted by GEP score

ord_s <- order(clinical$GEP)                    # patients: low to high GEP
ord_g <- order(cor(t(Z), clinical$GEP))         # genes: least to most correlated with the score
Zc <- pmax(pmin(Z, 2.5), -2.5)                  # cap for display only

hm <- data.frame(sample = factor(rep(colnames(Zc), each = nrow(Zc)), levels = colnames(Zc)[ord_s]),
                 gene   = factor(rep(rownames(Zc), ncol(Zc)), levels = rownames(Zc)[ord_g]),
                 z      = as.vector(Zc))
p_hm <- ggplot(hm, aes(sample, gene, fill = z)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#0072B2", mid = "white", high = "#D55E00", midpoint = 0) +
  labs(x = "Patients (sorted by GEP score)", y = NULL, fill = "z-score") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
        panel.grid = element_blank())

strip <- data.frame(sample = factor(clinical$sample_id, levels = colnames(Zc)[ord_s]),
                    BOR = clinical$BOR)
p_strip <- ggplot(strip, aes(sample, 1, fill = BOR)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(NR = "grey90", R = "#D55E00")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Response") +
  theme_void()

p_heat <- p_strip / p_hm + plot_layout(heights = c(1, 12), guides = "collect")
p_heat
ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "gep_heatmap.png"), p_heat, width = 10, height = 5.5, dpi = 300)
```

**Analysis:** The heatmap shows a clear gradient: patients go from
"cold" (all genes low) to "inflamed" (all genes high). The only
exceptions are HLA-DQA1 and CD276, as expected. We can observe that
responders are more frequent on the right, but they are not all there,
and many non-responders also have a high GEP. This graph suggests that
high GEP is a factor favouring response to the treatment, but not a
sufficient condition.

## 3. Test whether patients with a higher GEP score are more likely to respond

To investigate whether the GEP distribution differ between responders
and non responders, we first compare the two groups with a Wilcoxon
test. Then we fit a logistic regression. We do not use a Cox regression:
Cox models a time to event (survival), while our outcome is binary (R or
NR). Logistic regression models the probability of response directly.

```{r}
# GEP score in responders vs non-responders

wt <- wilcox.test(GEP ~ BOR, data = clinical)
wt

p_box <- ggplot(clinical, aes(BOR, GEP, fill = BOR)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, size = 1, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(NR = "grey70", R = "#D55E00")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "GEP score",
       subtitle = paste("Wilcoxon p =", signif(wt$p.value, 2))) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
p_box
ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "gep_boxplot_response.png"), p_box, width = 4, height = 4, dpi = 300)
```

The test p-value (0.00018) shows a clear association between GEP score
and response: responders have higher GEP scores than non-responders.

```{r}
# Logistic regression: response ~ GEP

fit <- glm(resp ~ GEP, data = clinical, family = binomial)
summary(fit)

# Odds ratio for a 1-unit increase in GEP score, with 95% CI
exp(cbind(OR = coef(fit), confint.default(fit)))["GEP", ]
```

**Analysis:** The logistic regression confirms the Wilcoxon test. The
GEP coefficient is positive and significant (p = 0.0003). The odds ratio
is 3.1 (95% CI 1.7 to 5.8): when the GEP score increases by 1, the odds
of response are multiplied by about 3. The GEP score has a standard
deviation of 0.75, so 1 unit is a large step (from a "cold" to a clearly
"inflamed" tumour). But the confidence interval is wide because we only
have 25 responders.

## 4. Interpret the result and discuss why a high GEP does not guarantee response

In the paper, Ayers et al. describe the GEP as "necessary but not
sufficient" for response. Non-responders fall into two groups: tumours
without T-cell inflammation (cold) and inflamed tumours that still do
not respond. We will try to check whether the same pattern is visible
here.

```{r}
# Table of response rate for GEP above/below median

clinical$GEP_group <- ifelse(clinical$GEP > median(clinical$GEP), "GEP high", "GEP low")

tab <- table(clinical$GEP_group, clinical$BOR)
tab

# Response rate in each group (%)
round(100 * prop.table(tab, margin = 1), 1)

fisher.test(tab)
```

We obtain again a promising result, with a significant p-value,
suggesting that a high GEP has a positive impact on the response rate.
Let's take the investigation further with a graph.

TMB (tumour mutational burden) is a second biomarker. It reflects how
many neoantigens the tumour can show to T cells. If the GEP is
"necessary but not sufficient", we expect responders among GEP-high
patients mainly when TMB is also high. TMB is missing for some patients,
so they are left out of this plot.

```{r}
# GEP score versus TMB

tmb_df <- clinical[!is.na(clinical$TMB), ]
cat("Patients with TMB:", nrow(tmb_df), "of", nrow(clinical), "\n")

p_tmb <- ggplot(tmb_df, aes(GEP, TMB, colour = BOR)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median(clinical$GEP), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = median(tmb_df$TMB), linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_y_continuous(trans = "log1p") +   # log(1 + TMB), because some patients have TMB = 0
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(NR = "grey60", R = "#D55E00")) +
  labs(x = "GEP score", y = "TMB (log scale)", colour = "Response") +
  theme_bw()
p_tmb
ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "gep_vs_tmb.png"), p_tmb, width = 6, height = 4.5, dpi = 300)

# Response rate in the four quadrants (cut at the medians)
tmb_df$TMB_group <- ifelse(tmb_df$TMB > median(tmb_df$TMB), "TMB high", "TMB low")
tmb_df$GEP_group <- ifelse(tmb_df$GEP > median(clinical$GEP), "GEP high", "GEP low")
aggregate(resp ~ GEP_group + TMB_group, data = tmb_df,
          FUN = function(x) c(n = length(x), responders = sum(x), rate = round(100 * mean(x), 1)))
```

**Analysis:** This plot is very informative. The two median lines split
the patients into four groups: both low GEP score and TMB, high TMB and
low GEP score, high GEP score and low TMB, and both high. Most of the
responders (15 of the 21 with a TMB value) belong to the last group. In
the "high GEP, low TMB" group, only 2 of 35 patients respond. This shows
that having a high GEP score is not sufficient: having a high TMB seems
to be another condition for showing response to the treatment.

However, in the high TMB and high GEP score category, more than half of
the patients are still non responders: it suggests that other factors
are necessary to favour response. In the class we mentioned a third
biomarker, the PD-1 / PD-L1 axis. PD-1 (PDCD1) is on the T cells, and
PD-L1 (CD274) is the target of atezolizumab. Both genes are already part
of the GEP, so they are strongly correlated with the score.But it is
still informative to look at them inside the "high GEP, high TMB" group,
to see if they help separate responders from non-responders.

```{r}
# Investigate PD-1 (PDCD1) and PD-L1 (CD274) expression as other co-factors

# Patients with both high GEP and high TMB
hh <- tmb_df[tmb_df$GEP_group == "GEP high" & tmb_df$TMB_group == "TMB high", ]
table(hh$BOR)

hh$PDCD1 <- logtpm["PDCD1", hh$sample_id]
hh$CD274 <- logtpm["CD274", hh$sample_id]

# Correlation of each gene with the GEP score (all patients)
cor(logtpm["PDCD1", ], clinical$GEP, method = "spearman")
cor(logtpm["CD274", ], clinical$GEP, method = "spearman")

# R vs NR inside the "high GEP, high TMB" group
wilcox.test(PDCD1 ~ BOR, data = hh)
wilcox.test(CD274 ~ BOR, data = hh)

hh_long <- data.frame(
  gene = rep(c("PDCD1 (PD-1)", "CD274 (PD-L1)"), each = nrow(hh)),
  expr = c(hh$PDCD1, hh$CD274),
  BOR  = rep(hh$BOR, 2)
)
p_pd1 <- ggplot(hh_long, aes(BOR, expr, fill = BOR)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, size = 1, alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ gene, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(NR = "grey70", R = "#D55E00")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "log2(TPM + 1)", subtitle = "Patients with high GEP and high TMB") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
p_pd1
ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, "gep_pd1_pdl1.png"), p_pd1, width = 6, height = 4, dpi = 300)
```

Inside the "high GEP, high TMB" group, responders have slightly higher
PD-1 and PD-L1 expression, but the difference is not significant (p =
0.15 for PDCD1, p = 0.10 for CD274). With only 38 patients (15
responders), the test has little power. Also, both genes are highly
correlated with the GEP score (rho = 0.92 and 0.83), so they bring
little new information. As a conclusion, other factors, not measured by
the GEP, probably matter.

## 5. Summary and interpretation

**Is the GEP associated with response?** Yes. Responders have a higher
GEP score than non-responders (Wilcoxon p = 0.00018). In the logistic
regression, the odds of response are about 3 times higher per unit of
GEP (OR 3.1, 95% CI 1.7 to 5.8). Patients above the median GEP respond
in 21% of cases, against 5% below the median (Fisher p = 0.002). Most of
the 18 genes go in the same directon: 15 of them are higher in
responders (FDR \< 0.05). This agrees with Ayers et al. and with the
course

**Why does a high GEP not guarantee response?** Even in the GEP-high
group, 79% of patients do not respond. The GEP is "necessary but not
sufficient":

**Biological explanations:** - The GEP measures T-cell presence, not
tumour recognition. T cells can be in the tumour without recognising it.
TMB is a proxy for neoantigens, and GEP and TMB give complementary
information. With a high GEP but a low TMB, only 2 of 35 patients
respond, but with both high, the rate rises to 39%. - Other resistance
mechanisms: Mariathasan et al. showed that TGF-β signalling in
fibroblasts excludes T cells from the tumour in IMvigor210. Other
mechanisms can also block the response, for example loss of antigen
presentation (B2M, HLA) or other checkpoints (LAG3, TIGIT). The GEP does
not capture them, so those are probably the missing factors that I was
looking for in task 4

**Limitations.** We have only 25 responders, so the confidence intervals
are wide. TMB is missing for 42 patients. Also, we work with bulk
RNA-seq that mixes tumour, immune and stromal cells, so the score does
not tell where the T cells are.
